title: AnyLoss: Transforming Classification Metrics into Loss Functions

problem.claim: Many binary-classification evaluation metrics are derived from confusion matrices in non-differentiable form, making it difficult to create loss functions that directly optimize them.

gap.claim: The lack of solutions for directly optimizing confusion-matrix-based metrics hinders difficult tasks such as imbalanced learning and necessitates computationally expensive hyperparameter search during model selection.

contributions.claim: AnyLoss transforms confusion-matrix-based metrics into loss functions usable in optimization processes.
The approach uses an approximation function to represent the confusion matrix differentiably, enabling direct use of the resulting metrics as loss functions.
The paper provides the mechanism of the approximation function and proves differentiability by suggesting derivatives of the loss functions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments using diverse neural networks and many datasets, demonstrating general availability for targeting confusion-matrix-based metrics.
The authors report outstanding performance on imbalanced datasets.
The authors report competitive learning speed relative to multiple baseline models and characterize the method as efficient.

narrative_sequence.summary: Binary-classification models can be assessed with many evaluation metrics.
Most such metrics are non-differentiable because they are derived from confusion matrices.
This limitation hinders difficult tasks such as imbalanced learning and increases reliance on expensive hyperparameter search.
AnyLoss transforms confusion-matrix-based metrics into loss functions by using a differentiable approximation of the confusion matrix.
The paper reports theoretical differentiability and experiments indicating broad applicability, strong imbalanced-learning results, and competitive learning speed.

source_observation.claim: A differentiable approximation can make confusion-matrix-based metrics directly usable as training objectives.

interpretation.claim: When evaluation metrics are difficult to optimize directly, a differentiable surrogate representation may bridge evaluation and training.

application.claim: This pattern may support metric-oriented optimization in settings such as imbalanced classification.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that the approach works equally well for every metric, dataset, model, or task.

unknowns: The specific approximation function and derivative forms are not given.
The evaluated metrics, datasets, neural-network architectures, baselines, and quantitative results are not specified.
The abstract does not report computational costs or limitations beyond the stated learning-speed comparison.
